analysis.one_liner: Trades antitrust immunity for state licensing boards if states curb licensing abuses and prefer lighter rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Issa with one cosponsor in July 2017, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and a subcommittee and died there without ever receiving a vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2015 Supreme Court ruling exposed state occupational licensing boards to antitrust lawsuits when board members use their power to squeeze out competitors. This bill would give those boards immunity from antitrust law again, but only in states that agree to reforms: adopting a policy of using the lightest regulation that protects the public, creating an office that must approve board actions in writing, or letting workers challenge licensing rules in court with attorney fees if they win. In effect, it offers states a bargain: tame your licensing boards, and they get legal protection.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to enter licensed occupations, consumers who pay licensing-driven prices, entrepreneurs with new business models, and military spouses seeking license reciprocity. The bill would make it easier to challenge licensing rules in state court and shift the burden to the state to prove a license is truly needed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers facing licensing barriers

how_it_helps.text: The bill's own findings state that occupational licensing has grown partly because private interests sought it to limit competition, and that it often limits workers' opportunities, frustrates entrepreneurs, and raises consumer prices [S3].

States wanting board immunity must adopt a policy of using less restrictive alternatives to licensing, such as inspections, bonding, registration, or voluntary certification, whenever those suffice to protect public health and safety [S3].

Under one route, states must create an Office of Supervision of Occupational Boards that reviews and must approve or reject board rules in writing, investigates complaints, and can terminate enforcement actions that don't serve the public-interest policy [S3].

Under the other route, states must let individuals defend themselves against licensing enforcement and sue for injunctions; once a plaintiff shows a rule burdens their work, the state must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the rule protects against real, substantial threats and is the least restrictive option, with attorney fees awarded to successful challengers [S3].

States must periodically review existing licensing rules, comparing other states' approaches and evaluating reciprocity compacts and recognizing licenses held by spouses of active-duty military members [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State governments would bear the cost of new supervision offices, periodic reviews, and attorney fees to successful challengers. Professional licensing boards and incumbent licensees would give up enforcement powers they now use to limit competition, and would lose the antitrust protection courts had stripped away unless their states reform.

drawbacks.text: The core trade is real: the bill grants antitrust immunity to boards, so in states that take the deal, some anticompetitive actions by board members would escape the antitrust liability the Supreme Court imposed in 2015, with the safeguards resting on state political will [S3].

The judicial-review route imposes a demanding standard, requiring the state to prove licensing rules are justified by clear and convincing evidence, which could also weaken health and safety rules that most experts agree are necessary [S3].

States would face new administrative costs to build supervision offices and run five-year review cycles covering all licensed occupations, and could simply decline to comply, leaving board immunity in limbo [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The pro-competition gains for workers and consumers are genuine and the reform conditions are unusually substantive, not decorative. The honest objection is that immunity is a real prize handed to boards dominated by industry members, and the bill's heavy evidentiary standards could sweep away some legitimate safety licensing along with the protectionist kind. On balance it pushes harder against incumbent-driven licensing than anything in current law, but it was never debated, so none of these trade-offs got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee on regulatory reform, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA) introduced the Restoring Board Immunity Act on July 27, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
One Republican cosponsored the bill; no Democrats signed on [S4].
On September 6, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law — the last action recorded for the bill [S5].

The bill was written in response to the Supreme Court's 2015 decision in North Carolina State Board of Dental Examiners v. FTC, which held that licensing boards controlled by market participants can face antitrust liability and left states uncertain how to protect their boards [S3].
No markup, hearing, or floor vote ever occurred before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, killing the bill under Congress's rule that legislation dies at the end of a Congress [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State licensing boards and the incumbent professionals who sit on them came out ahead: they kept their existing enforcement powers without any new requirement to justify licenses, and they never had to choose between reforming and facing antitrust suits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent licensees and state licensing boards

for.name: Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, framing it as a way to combat licensing abuse by economic incumbents and restore board immunity through state reform [S1][S3][S5].

for.name: One Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor [S4].

against.role: Chair and committee of referral, House Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in July 2017 and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or floor vote; the bill died in committee [S5].

against.name: Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in September 2017 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to reveal a split; sponsorship was entirely Republican (Issa plus one Republican cosponsor, no Democrats), and no recorded opposition ever materialized because the bill never left committee [S4][S5].

industries.note: Boards would regain the antitrust immunity they lost after the 2015 Supreme Court ruling, but only if their state adopts a least-restrictive-regulation policy and subjects every board action to written approval by a supervision office or to strict judicial review [S3]. Their interest in keeping enforcement power and avoiding liability runs against consumers and would-be workers, who benefit when boards cannot block competitors [S3].

Licensed incumbents use board authority to limit entry and police competition; the bill's findings say private interests have sought licensing for exactly this purpose [S3]. It would narrow what boards can enforce, add court challenges with attorney fees against incumbents' boards, and leave antitrust liability in place for states that do not reform [S3].

industries.industry: New entrants and small service businesses competing against licensees
industries.note: Entrepreneurs in fields like teeth whitening, hair braiding, or casket sales — frequently targets of board enforcement — would gain written-approval safeguards, a right to defend against enforcement, and injunctions against rules that burden their work [S3]. Their interest in entering the market matches consumers' interest in lower prices and more choices [S3].

States would pay for a new supervision office or court procedures, periodic five-year reviews of all licensed occupations, and attorney fees to successful challengers, but gain a clear federal route to protect their boards from antitrust suits and tools to cut costly, unnecessary licensing [S3].
